title: Website Migration Without Losing SEO: A Step-by-Step Checklist
metaTitle: Website Migration SEO Checklist: Keep Your Rankings
metaDescription: Moving to a new platform, design or domain? Follow this checklist for redirects, content, tracking and post-launch checks so your rankings survive.
excerpt: A new website should grow your traffic, but a careless launch can wipe out years of rankings in a week. This checklist covers what to do before, during and after a migration so search engines carry your history across to the new site.

faqs.q: Will I lose rankings when I redesign or move my website?
faqs.a: Some short-term movement is normal while search engines process the changes, but lasting losses are avoidable. They usually come from missing redirects, removed content, changed page titles or pages accidentally blocked from indexing. With a full redirect map, preserved content and checks after launch, most sites recover within a few weeks and often improve.

faqs.q: What is a 301 redirect and why does it matter in a migration?
faqs.a: A 301 redirect tells browsers and search engines that a page has moved permanently to a new address. It sends visitors to the right place and passes most of the old page's ranking strength to the new one. Without it, the old address returns an error, the page drops out of search results and any links pointing to it are wasted.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to recover after a website migration?
faqs.a: For a well-planned migration on the same domain, rankings typically settle within two to six weeks. A change of domain takes longer, often a few months, because search engines have to transfer trust to the new address. Large sites take longer than small ones because there are more pages to recrawl.

faqs.q: Should I change my URLs during a redesign?
faqs.a: Only if there is a clear benefit. Every changed URL needs a redirect and carries some risk, so keeping existing addresses is the safest option. If the old structure is messy or the new platform forces a change, map every old URL to its closest new equivalent and redirect it individually.

body:
A website migration is any change that alters how search engines see your site: a new platform, a redesign, a new domain, a move to HTTPS, or a restructure of your pages. Done well, it improves speed, design and rankings together. Done carelessly, it can erase years of search visibility in days.

The risk is not the new website. It is the handover between the old one and the new one. This checklist covers that handover in three stages.

## Why migrations lose traffic

Search engines know your site as a set of addresses, each with its own history, content and links from other sites. When those addresses change or vanish, that history is lost unless you tell search engines where everything went.

The usual causes of a traffic drop are predictable:

- Old addresses that return errors because nobody redirected them.
- Pages that ranked well but were dropped or merged in the redesign.
- Page titles, headings and text rewritten without regard to what they ranked for.
- A staging setting that blocks search engines, left switched on after launch.
- Tracking that stopped working, so nobody noticed the drop.

Every one of these is avoidable.

## Before launch: take stock

**Crawl the existing site and export every URL.** Combine three sources: a crawl of the site, the pages listed in Google Search Console, and the pages that receive traffic in your analytics. Old pages that are no longer linked in the menu often still rank and receive visitors.

**Record your baseline.** Note current rankings for your main keywords, organic traffic by page, and the number of indexed pages. Without a baseline you cannot tell whether the migration helped or hurt.

**Identify your most valuable pages.** Sort by organic traffic and by the number of links from other sites. These pages need the most care: keep their content, their titles and, where possible, their addresses.

**Build the redirect map.** List every old URL beside the new URL it should lead to. Match each to its closest equivalent, not to the home page. Redirecting everything to the home page tells search engines the old content is gone, and its rankings go with it.

**Keep what ranks.** Carry over the page titles, descriptions, headings and body text of pages that perform. Improve them if you like, but do not replace a page that ranks with a shorter one that says less.

**Check the new site before it goes live.** On the staging version, confirm that each page has a unique title and description, one main heading, working internal links, correct canonical tags, structured data, and image alt text. If you publish in more than one language, check the language tags too.

## At launch: switch over cleanly

- Put the redirects live at the same moment as the new site, as permanent (301 or 308) redirects.
- Remove any setting that blocks search engines. Check robots.txt and look for "noindex" tags left over from staging.
- Confirm analytics and conversion tracking record a test visit and a test purchase or enquiry.
- Submit the new XML sitemap in Google Search Console.
- Test a sample of old addresses by hand, including the most valuable pages, and confirm each lands on the right new page in a single step.
- Check the site on a phone, and check page speed. A redesign that is heavier than the old site can lose rankings on speed alone.

If you are changing domain, also use the change of address tool in Google Search Console, and keep the old domain registered and redirecting for at least a year.

## After launch: watch closely

The first four weeks decide the outcome. Check these at least weekly.

- **Crawl errors.** Search Console's page indexing report lists addresses that return "not found". Each one with traffic or links needs a redirect.
- **Indexed pages.** The count should move towards the number of real pages on the new site.
- **Rankings and traffic.** Compare against your baseline. A small dip in the first two weeks is normal. A steep or continuing drop means something is wrong.
- **Redirect chains.** A redirect that leads to another redirect slows crawling. Point each old address straight at its final destination.
- **Conversions.** Traffic can hold steady while enquiries fall, if a form or checkout broke in the move.

Keep the redirects in place permanently. Removing them after a few months undoes the work.

## Platform-specific points

Moving between platforms adds its own details. A move to [Shopify](/development/shopify/) changes the URL structure of products and collections, so the redirect map matters even more. A [WordPress](/development/wordpress/) rebuild often changes category and tag addresses. A move to a [custom-built site](/development/custom-development/) gives full control over URLs, which makes it possible to keep the old addresses exactly.

Whichever platform you choose, the question to ask your developers is the same: what happens to every existing address? Our comparison of [Shopify and custom builds](/blog/shopify-vs-custom-ecommerce/) covers how to choose between them.

## When a hacked or neglected site is part of the picture

If the old site was hacked, it may have left behind hundreds of spam pages in Google's index. Do not redirect those to your real pages. Let them return a "gone" response so search engines drop them, check Search Console for unfamiliar users and sitemaps, and remove the old installation entirely once you have what you need from it.

## The short version

Know every URL you have. Decide where each one goes. Keep the content that ranks. Launch the redirects with the site. Then watch the numbers for a month and fix what appears.

At TDM, migrations are planned jointly by the developers who build the new site and the [SEO](/marketing/seo/) team who protect the rankings, which is how the redirect map gets built before launch instead of after the traffic drops.
